title: The Balance Fallacy
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: The author argues against the common instinct in education debates to split the difference -- 'you can have both' -- on questions like seating arrangements, inquiry vs. explicit teaching, and hands-on learning vs. writing. Using the specific example of classroom seating, the piece argues that with roughly 27% of Australian students carrying a diagnosed or imputed disability, evidence that row seating raises on-task behaviour from 35% to 70% for students with additional needs means the question is not aesthetic preference but equity, and there is no legitimate 'balance' between what helps and what harms vulnerable students. The same logic is extended to inquiry vs. explicit teaching, citing Kirschner, Sweller and Clark's 2006 paper to argue novices lack the background knowledge to benefit from inquiry, and that explicit instruction must precede any inquiry rather than being blended with it throughout a unit. A confessional anecdote about a failed hands-on economics simulation illustrates the author's broader claim that 'experience does not equate to learning' -- that activity-based tasks often direct students' attention to the doing rather than the intended concept. The piece closes by arguing that reflexive calls for 'balance' or nuance in pedagogy debates actually muddy professional standards and give cover to practices that are not backed by evidence.
points: The author cites data that seating in rows raises on-task behaviour from 35% to 70% for students with additional needs, and treats classroom seating as a question of equity rather than teacher preference.

The piece leans on Kirschner, Sweller and Clark's 2006 paper to argue novice students lack the background knowledge to benefit from inquiry learning, so explicit instruction must come first, not be blended throughout.

A first-person account of a failed 'countries and resources' economics simulation is used to argue that hands-on activities often focus students on the doing rather than the intended concept, so 'experience does not equate to learning.'

The author frames written work as a powerful cognitive tool because it 'codifies thinking while simultaneously cognitive offloading from our working memory,' pushing back on the idea that writing is optional busywork.
The piece explicitly rejects 'balance' as a legitimate default position in pedagogy debates, arguing it muddies professional standards rather than reflecting genuine even-handedness.
quotes: 27% of students in Australia have either a diagnosed or imputed disability as per the NCCD. These students require an educational environment which minimises extraneous load and limits to their attention if they are able to access the instruction on the same level as their peers.

There are studies which have shown that rows increase on task behaviour from 35% to 70% for students for students with additional needs. When we work in an era where teachers WILL have students with additional needs in their room and the likelihood of more than 1 in 4 students having some level of additional needs, the evidence supports seating which supports their inclusion.

This is an absolute nightmare for equity as those students with additional needs already lack the privilege of prior knowledge that their peers may come pre-loaded with therefore increasing the attainment gap.

The problem here is that by 'learning by doing' the students were no actually focussed on the learning, they were focussed on the doing. This activity based planning did not actually draw their attention to what they were supposed to be learning and therefore learning did not occur.

Writing codifies thinking while simultaneously cognitive offloading from our working memory. It allows students to rehearse what they currently know, create new ideas and then review and revise the writing to improve upon it.
At the end of the day, it is your professional responsibility to stand for something and back up the thing you stand for with reasonable evidence.
